title: Choose Your Thesis Methodology: 7 Decisions
description: Seven decisions for aligning thesis questions, evidence, research design, data collection, analysis, feasibility and ethics.

pages.heading: Choosing a Thesis Methodology? Make These 7 Decisions
pages.text: A defensible methodology shows how each research question becomes trustworthy evidence—not simply which technique sounds advanced.
pages.alt: Postgraduate engineering student connecting a research question to sensor evidence and a methodology pathway

pages.heading: 1. Start With the Research Question
pages.text: Define the phenomenon, context, objective and answer you need. Your method should serve that question; it should not force the question to fit a favorite tool.
pages.alt: Engineering student narrowing a broad thesis topic into one precise research question

pages.heading: 2. Decide What Evidence You Need
pages.text: Use quantitative evidence for measurable patterns, qualitative evidence for experiences and context, or mixed methods when both are needed to answer the question.
pages.alt: Researcher comparing quantitative, qualitative and mixed forms of engineering evidence

pages.heading: 3. Choose the Research Design
pages.text: Match experiment, simulation, survey or case study to the claim. A causal question needs different control and evidence than a descriptive or exploratory one.
pages.alt: Student comparing experiment, simulation, survey and case-study research designs

pages.heading: 4. Define Sampling and Collection
pages.text: Specify the population or test conditions, variables, sample logic, instruments, calibration and collection procedure before gathering results.
pages.alt: Student arranging samples, calibration tools and sensors for a data-collection plan

pages.heading: 5. Plan the Analysis Before Collection
pages.text: Choose metrics, statistical tests or coding rules in advance. This checks whether the planned evidence can answer the question and reduces data-driven improvisation.
pages.alt: Engineering researcher planning analysis with abstract charts before collecting data

pages.heading: 6. Test Feasibility and Ethics
pages.text: Check time, equipment, skills, approvals, safety, privacy and consent. Pilot the hardest step early enough to revise the plan responsibly.
pages.alt: Student piloting a safe engineering study while participants review blank consent cards

pages.heading: 7. Justify and Document Every Choice
pages.text: Explain why each method fits, record limitations and document justified changes. Traceability makes the study easier to assess and reproduce.
pages.alt: Researcher documenting changes between two engineering test setups

pages.heading: Methodology Is a Traceable Argument
pages.text: Question to evidence. Evidence to design. Design to analysis. Keep every choice aligned, feasible, ethical and visible.
pages.alt: Prepared engineering student reviewing a complete and traceable thesis methodology
